content: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends the use of combination therapy to treat malaria in order to prevent the development of drug resistance. Azithromycin, an antibiotic with antimalarial properties, has been proposed as a potential option for antimalarial therapy. This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of azithromycin, either as monotherapy or in combination with other antimalarial drugs, compared to alternative antimalarial treatments for uncomplicated malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum or Plasmodium vivax. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, up to August 2010. They also reviewed conference proceedings, reference lists, and contacted researchers and a pharmaceutical company. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials that compared azithromycin (alone or in combination) with other antimalarial drugs or combinations. The primary outcome was treatment failure by day 28, defined as parasitological or clinical evidence of treatment failure. Secondary outcomes included treatment failure corrected for new infections (confirmed by PCR), fever and parasite clearance times, and adverse events. Fifteen trials involving 2,284 participants (69% male, 16% children) met the inclusion criteria. These studies were conducted in various malaria-endemic regions, including Thailand, India, South America, Africa, and Asia. The trials included 41 treatment arms, 12 different drugs, and 28 treatment regimens. Two studies specifically examined P. vivax. Azithromycin monotherapy for three days showed poor efficacy for both P. vivax and P. falciparum. For P. vivax, the failure rate was 56% (95% CI 31–78) with a daily dose of 0.5 g in Thailand, and 12% (95% CI 7–21) with a daily dose of 1 g in India. For P. falciparum, the failure rate was 64% (95% CI 36–86) with a daily dose of 1 g in India. A combination of 1 g azithromycin and 0.6 g chloroquine daily for three days for uncomplicated P. falciparum infections was associated with higher treatment failure rates in India and Indonesia compared to the combination of sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine and chloroquine (pooled RR 2.66, 95% CI 1.25–5.67). Similarly, this combination showed increased failure rates compared to atovaquone-proguanil in a multicenter trial conducted in Colombia and Suriname (RR 24.72, 95% CI 6.16–99.20). However, no increased risk of treatment failure was observed in two African studies where mefloquine was the comparator drug (pooled RR 2.02, 95% CI 0.51–7.96, P = 0.3). For PCR-corrected data, the pooled RR for azithromycin/chloroquine versus mefloquine was 1.01 (95% CI 0.18–5.84, P = 1.0). An increased risk of treatment failure was observed when azithromycin (1.2–1.5 g) was combined with artesunate (200 mg daily for three days) and compared to artemether-lumefantrine (pooled RR 3.08, 95% CI 2.09–4.55; PCR-corrected pooled RR 3.63, 95% CI 2.02–6.52). Serious adverse events and treatment discontinuation rates were similar across treatment arms. However, more adverse events were reported when the azithromycin/chloroquine combination was compared to mefloquine (pooled RR 1.20, 95% CI 1.06–1.36) or atovaquone-proguanil (RR 1.41, 95% CI 1.09–1.83). In conclusion, there is currently no evidence to support the superiority or equivalence of azithromycin, either as monotherapy or in combination, for the treatment of P. falciparum or P. vivax compared to other antimalarial drugs or first-line antimalarial combinations. The available data suggest that azithromycin is a weak antimalarial agent, albeit with favorable safety characteristics. Unless further optimization of dosing, formulation, or product development results in a universally effective treatment, or a specific niche application is identified, azithromycin's role in malaria treatment appears limited.
